patient.case_title: 58F type 2 diabetes, poor control, hidden non-adherence
patient.name: Maria Alvarez
patient.chief_complaint: I'm thirsty all the time and I'm up all night going to the bathroom.

domains.name: Opening and purpose
domains.label: Competent
domains.rationale: You introduced yourself and your role and opened with a broad question. You did not set an agenda for the visit.

evidence.quote: I'm Sam, a nurse practitioner student. What brings you in today?
evidence.speaker: learner

domains.name: Rapport, respect, and empathy
domains.label: Developing
domains.rationale: You acknowledged how tiring her symptoms were early on, but when she told you she was scared you moved straight to allergies.

evidence.quote: That sounds exhausting.

evidence.quote: Do you have any allergies?
evidence.speaker: learner

domains.name: Information gathering
domains.label: Developing
domains.rationale: Your question about a normal day of eating and drinking was concrete and brought out the sweet tea. The adherence question was closed and judgmental, and you never asked about family history, side effects, or cost.

evidence.quote: Walk me through what you eat and drink on a normal day.
evidence.speaker: learner

evidence.quote: Are you taking it like you're supposed to?
evidence.speaker: learner

domains.label: Developing
domains.rationale: She looked away while saying she takes her metformin every day, and she was visibly frightened at t9. Neither was followed up.

domains.name: Explanation and shared decisions
domains.label: Developing
domains.rationale: You gave the result as a number and called it high without explaining what it means or asking what she made of it.

evidence.quote: Your HbA1c is 9.2 percent, which is high.
evidence.speaker: learner

domains.name: Clinical reasoning and synthesis
domains.label: Unsafe or absent
domains.rationale: The plan to raise the dose rests on an adherence claim you did not check. An HbA1c of 9.2% on a drug she says she takes daily should have prompted a look at the refill history.

evidence.quote: Since you're already taking the metformin every day, we'll probably need to raise the dose.
evidence.speaker: learner

domains.name: Professionalism, safety, and closure
domains.label: Competent
domains.rationale: You were courteous, deferred the dose decision to your preceptor, and gave a follow-up interval. You did not check her understanding or invite questions.

evidence.quote: I'll talk to my preceptor and we'll see you in three months.
evidence.speaker: learner

strength.text: Asking her to walk you through a normal day got an honest, specific answer about sweet tea that a yes/no diet question would have missed.

evidence.quote: Walk me through what you eat and drink on a normal day.
evidence.speaker: learner

important_gap.text: You accepted that she takes metformin daily and built the plan on it. The refill history, which you did not open, shows two fills in six months.

evidence.quote: Great, that's good to hear.
evidence.speaker: learner

safety_or_accuracy_concern.text: Raising the dose of a drug she is mostly not taking, for a reason that is partly its side effects, risks making adherence worse.

objectives.feedback: A question that implies there is a right answer invites the right answer. Try asking what taking it is like for her, or how many doses she misses in a typical week.
objectives.description: Recognise that reported adherence does not fit the chart, and find out why.

objectives.feedback: She told you she was scared and you answered with a number. Naming the fear and asking what she is afraid of would have opened the conversation about her mother.
objectives.description: Notice and respond to the patient's fear about where her diabetes is heading.

behaviors.feedback: Her fear at t9 went unanswered.
A high HbA1c alongside reported daily metformin was not questioned.

strengths: Concrete, open question about a normal day of eating and drinking.
Clear introduction of yourself and your role.
improvements: Ask about adherence without implying a right answer.
Stop and respond when the patient shows fear.
next_attempt_suggestions: Before proposing a medication change, open the refill history.
When her face changes, say what you see and ask about it.

transcript.text: Hi Mrs. Alvarez, I'm Sam, a nurse practitioner student. What brings you in today?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: I'm thirsty all the time and I'm up all night going to the bathroom.

transcript.speaker: learner
transcript.text: That sounds exhausting. How long has that been going on?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: About three months now. It keeps getting worse.

transcript.speaker: learner
transcript.text: Walk me through what you eat and drink on a normal day.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Whatever's left at the cafeteria, mostly. And my sweet tea, four or five big glasses.

transcript.speaker: learner
transcript.text: I see you're on metformin. Are you taking it like you're supposed to?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Oh yes. I take my metformin every day.

transcript.speaker: learner
transcript.text: Great, that's good to hear. I'm going to order an HbA1c to see where your sugar has been.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Okay. Is it bad? I just... I'm scared of where this is heading.

transcript.speaker: learner
transcript.text: Your HbA1c is 9.2 percent, which is high. Do you have any allergies?

transcript.speaker: learner
transcript.text: Since you're already taking the metformin every day, we'll probably need to raise the dose. I'll talk to my preceptor and we'll see you in three months.
